name: Malagasy, western and southwestern dialects, incl. Mahafaly and Tanalana
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.

catalog_locator: Howe 2017 §2.3.6 'Stress', pp. 48-49, footnotes 12-13; dialect grouping p. 23 ('the Southwestern group includes Masikoro, Vezo, Mahafaly and Tandroy'), Tanalana note p. 24. Adelaar 2019 p. 60 ('Malagasy stress is contrastive') and the two MHF forms tùmbukĕ (p. 73, entry 'Foot') and rànju (p. 74, entry 'Leg').
catalog_quote: While there are a handful of monosyllabic lexical items, most Malagasy roots are di- or trisyllabic. Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable. However, lexical items ending in one of the “weak final syllables” (-na, -ka, -tra in Merina; -ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952); -gnV, -kV, -trV¹² in North Betsimisaraka (O’Neill 2015) and Tsimihety (Dahl 1952; Tsimilaza 1981)) have antepenultimate stress, and a small number of words have final-syllable stress. The morphology is highly agglutinative, often resulting in very long words and stress shifts. ... Stress can be phonologically distinctive, as in the MO pairs tànana ‘hand’ — tanàna ‘village’ and làlana ‘road’ — lalàna ‘law’¹³. Suffixation processes typically cause shift of primary stress one syllable to the right. In longer words, certain syllables prior to the syllable bearing primary stress receive secondary stress. In compounds, primary stress [p. 49] occurs on the original stressed syllable of the rightmost component word ... [fn. 12: V indicates a vowel whose quality is determined according to vowel harmony processes ... fn. 13: Stress is not typically marked in the Malagasy orthography but for clarity in this work it will often be marked in orthographic forms by a grave accent (̀) above the syllable nucleus.] [p. 23] the Southwestern group includes Masikoro, Vezo, Mahafaly and Tandroy.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, second-hand for Mahafaly: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root; roots ending in a weak final syllable (in the south-western dialects, to which Mahafaly belongs, -ke, -tse; Adelaar's two Mahafaly forms show -kĕ behaving this way: tùmbukĕ, rànju) carry antepenultimate stress; a small number of roots are final-stressed. Suffixation moves primary stress one syllable to the right.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Howe p.48: 'In longer words, certain syllables prior to the syllable bearing primary stress receive secondary stress'; in compounds primary stress on the rightmost member, secondary on the others (p.49). Stated for Malagasy generally, not for Mahafaly.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak-final roots (-ke, -tse in SW dialects) = antepenultimate; a small number of final-stressed words; stress is lexically contrastive in minimal pairs (Merina examples).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (root) level, citation forms, with stress shift under suffixation. The statement is pan-Malagasy with an explicit sub-clause for 'western and southwestern dialects' credited to Dahl 1952; Mahafaly is placed in the Southwestern group on p.24. No Mahafaly-specific stress sentence exists in any opened source; Howe's own Mahafaly (Ejeda) word list (Table C.8) carries no stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog maha1309 'Mahafaly-Antanalana Malagasy' (dialects Mahafaly maha1311 and Antanalana/Tanalana anta1262, Ampanihy-Betioky-Onilahy region, SW Madagascar) has no ISO code and is subsumed under tdx 'Tandroy-Mahafaly Malagasy' (Glottolog tand1256), for which a separate check folder exists. The Howe 2017 statement quoted is pan-Malagasy with a sub-clause for 'western and southwestern dialects' (Dahl 1952); Howe's Southwestern group = Masikoro, Vezo, Mahafaly, Tandroy (p.24). Adelaar 2019's two stress-marked MHF forms are the only first-hand Mahafaly stress data opened.

sources.note: Lexicostatistic study whose dataset has separate 'Mahafaly' and 'Antanalana' variants (p.11) - the basis of Glottolog's languoid name; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Alexander. 2019. On the history of Malagasy terms for human body parts. In V. V. Sikorsky & V. A. Pogadaev (eds), Malay-Indonesian Studies XXI (Festschrift A. K. Ogloblin), 53-89. Moscow.
sources.note: Stress marked on every polysyllable (p.60 'Malagasy stress is contrastive'); only two Mahafaly (MHF) forms in the paper: 'TDR, VEZ, MHF tùmbukĕ' (antepenult before weak final -kĕ) and 'TDR, MHF, S-SKL rànju' (penult), pp.82-83; MHF source row not recoverable from the text of Table 2; no rule statement for Mahafaly.

sources.note: English/Malagasy/Mahafaly phrasebook-glossary; index lists only phrase topics plus 'About the authors' (p.79); no pronunciation, accent or stress note; entries unaccented. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Ferrand, Gabriel. 1909. Essai de phonétique comparée du malais et des dialectes malgaches. Paris: Geuthner.
sources.note: 'Mahafali' is among the dialects surveyed (habitat note, forms passim); Chap. VI 'L'accent tonique' pp.236-245 states for Malagasy as a whole that disyllabic roots are 'généralement paroxytons, très rarement oxytons', trisyllabic roots 'généralement proparoxytons, quelquefois paroxytons'; no dialect-specific remark (no mention of Mahafali/dialecte/Sakalava/Bara inside the chapter).

sources.citation: Jully, Antony. 1901. Manuel des dialectes malgaches comprenant sept dialectes: hova, betsileo, tankarana, betsimisaraka, taimorona, tanosy, sakalava (mahafaly) et le soahely. Paris: J. André.
sources.note: The 'Sakalava' column is explicitly Mahafaly (p.VI 'le Sud ou Mahafaly'); the 'ACCENTUATION' section is only a typographic key (stressed syllable printed in italics, 'prononcée avec une pause et plus fortement que les autres'); italics are lost in the scanned; no rule of stress placement.
